question: to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

The Spanish Government has allegedly misappropriated over EUR 13 billion from the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) to pay pensions, minimum income benefits and even contributions to the postal service. Spain has decided to legalise the status of 500 000 people who entered the country illegally. A Spanish residence permit gives those concerned the right to visit other Schengen countries as tourists. Border controls will need to be introduced to monitor this. Furthermore, such mass regularisations are an incentive for more people to enter Europe illegally. Spain wants access to cheap EU SAFE funding, but it does not want to meet NATO’s 5 % defence spending target. Spain uses EU funds – to which Hungary also contributes – to finance a basic income that is twice as high as Hungarian social assistance, while Hungarian citizens lose their unemployment benefits after three months and are required to take part in public work schemes in exchange for significantly lower social benefits. 1.
Since when has the Commission been aware of these misappropriations, and what specific measures has it taken since they came to light? Please list all the measures.

What punitive measures are available to the Commission, and which of those does it intend to impose on Spain to prevent that country or other Member States from effectively stealing money that should be helping European taxpayers?

What specific conclusions is the Commission drawing from Spain’s actions in recent months regarding future European solidarity mechanisms, and what reforms of existing solidarity instruments are planned?
answer: EN E-001965/26 on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) The Commission is aware of the Spanish Court of Auditors’ observations that the legal basis for certain internal budget transfers ‘should have been more thoroughly justified’1. These do not call into question the lawful use of Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) funds under EU law but rather concern procedural requirements under Spanish budgetary law. While Spain’s Recovery and Resilience Plan supported the set up and reform of the national minimum income scheme ‘Ingreso Minimo Vital’ via Reform 5 (C22.R5)2, its management and implementation fall under the responsibility of the Member State, which fiscal aggregates must still comply with the EU’s economic governance framework. Furthermore, under Article 22 of the RRF Regulation3, the Commission may apply corrective measures where fraud, corruption or conflicts of interest in the implementation of the RRF are not corrected by the Member State. Based on current information, these situations do not concur in the instances highlighted by the Honourable Member. Under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/23234, Spain was identified as a Member State under migratory pressure for the first annual cycle of the permanent solidarity mechanism under the Asylum and Migration Management Regulation5. This will give it access to the 2026 Solidarity Pool, upon application of the Pact on Migration and Asylum under Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/26426. This is unrelated to Spain’s extraordinary regularisation process. Council Regulation (EU) 2025/11067 establishing the Security Action for Europe Regulation sets conditions for support to defence industry investments and does not link eligibility to NATO spending targets. Loan agreements, signed after each Council Implementing Decision, include required control and audit provisions under Article 223(4) of the Financial Regulation.
